title: Discovering Hidden Relationships of Alloy Properties with Manifold Learning
abstract: Abstract Establishing reliable correlations among material properties across different scales is essential for enabling informed materials selection, performance estimation, and property screening. While most existing datasets and modeling efforts focus on predicting individual properties from composition or microstructure, limited attention has been given to uncovering the interrelations between modulus-related, thermal, and strength properties. Although empirical relationships have been proposed to relate certain properties, these are limited to specific alloys and fail to generalize across scales. To address the challenge, this paper leverages machine learning (ML) to uncover hidden nonlinear relationships between properties. Firstly, 1731 experimentally validated alloys were curated from the ANSYS GRANTA database, and materials properties were categorized into thermally, mechanically, and strength-related groups. Three ML models are employed to learn relationships among alloy properties: neural networks (NN), geometric harmonics (GH), and double diffusion maps (DDM). Results demonstrate that thermal and mechanical properties are strongly interrelated and can be predicted with high accuracy. However, the strength property is revealed to be difficult to model due to the missing information on post-processing treatments. To address this, we incorporated treatment metadata for iron-based alloys. The inclusion of these data led to an increase of over 70% in the average  R 2 , highlighting that explicitly accounting for post-processing information is necessary to make strength prediction from other macroscopic properties practically reliable.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The rapid deployment of advanced alloys is central to progress in a wide range of technological applications in a multitude of fields such as the aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. Traditional experimental and computational methods for alloy development are slow, resource-intensive, and often limited in scope [ 4 ]. As a result, there has been a growing emphasis on data-driven approaches that can uncover hidden relationships among material properties and accelerate the materials design and development cycle [ 5 ,  6 ]. A central challenge in this domain is to establish reliable correlations between different material properties, particularly when they span multiple physical regimes, such as modulus-related, thermal, and strength-related behavior. Understanding these interdependencies not only aids in property prediction but also enables more informed material selection and targeted alloy optimization [ 7 ,  8 ]. While empirical formulas do exist to relate certain properties—such as hardness, shear modulus, and bulk modulus—these are typically limited to specific alloys and fail to generalize across all materials [ 9 ]. Recently, materials informatics efforts have largely focused on predicting individual properties from composition or microstructure [ 10 ,  11 ], but relatively few studies have explored the direct relationships between these properties themselves, especially across different scales and regimes. This gap presents an opportunity to explore innovative approaches that can uncover these relationships without the need for detailed microstructural data. This work demonstrates that strong cross-property predictions—particularly between modulus-related and thermal properties—can be achieved without composition or microstructure, enabling practical use in data-scarce (limited measured properties), legacy (older or incomplete datasets), or proprietary (non-disclosed composition) alloy systems. In practical engineering workflows, alloy chemistry and processing are often already defined, yet only a subset of macroscopic properties is experimentally characterized due to time and cost constraints. In such settings, the ability to infer unmeasured properties from available measurements provides a powerful mechanism for property completion, early-stage screening, and candidate down-selection, reducing experimental burden while accelerating materials development.

This paper investigates whether modulus, thermal, and strength properties of alloys can be correlated without relying on microstructural or compositional data. Specifically, we examine whether machine learning models can uncover these relationships using only experimental data. Machine learning excels in interpolation within a given design space but struggles with extrapolation, so it is crucial to utilize a dataset that spans a wide range of properties [ 12 ]. The research question is: Can we develop a generalizable framework that enables the prediction of additional macroscopic properties from a limited set of measured properties, without relying on costly experimental campaigns or first-principles analyses? This work addresses this question by a machine learning-based approach for correlating material properties across different alloys using purely experimental data, enabling macroscopic property inference and screening in partially characterized materials and reducing the need for extensive mechanical testing.

Existing research has long sought to establish empirical formulas that correlate material properties, such as the relationship between hardness and bulk modulus [ 13 ]. For example, Teter introduced an improved correlation between hardness and shear modulus [ 14 ], and others proposed macroscopic models that consider both shear modulus and bulk modulus to predict hardness [ 9 ,  15 ]. Another key avenue of research has focused on correlating hardness with strength properties, like yield strength [ 16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ] and tensile strength [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 – 21 ]. Despite their usefulness, these empirical relations often fail to generalize beyond specific alloys, limiting their applicability across diverse materials. In addition, theoretical parameters such as the Gru¨neisen parameter—which combines the thermal expansion coefficient, bulk modulus, density, and specific heat capacity—have been utilized to estimate missing properties [ 22 ]. Furthermore, the theory of elasticity can be used to correlate modulus-related properties and Poisson’s ratio [ 23 ]. Bassetti et al. proposed a method that uses weighted linear combinations of thermal, modulus, and strength properties to estimate missing values in alloys. However, this approach is constrained by its assumption of linearity in log–log space, which may fail to capture the more complex, nonlinear relationships that exist between properties [ 24 ]. These limitations highlight a critical gap, underscoring the need for innovative methods capable of capturing the intricate correlations between modulus, thermal, and strength properties across a broad spectrum of alloys—without relying on microstructural data or composition. Specifically, a successful approach must capture nonlinear cross-property dependencies between these regimes and remain transferable across diverse alloy classes, where simple empirical correlations often fail to generalize.

Recent advancements in machine learning (ML) provide powerful tools to model complex, nonlinear interactions in high-dimensional materials datasets. While machine learning has been widely applied to predict material properties, very few studies have focused on establishing direct correlations between macroscopic properties without relying on microscopic features or compositional descriptors [ 2 ,  25 ]. One of the few such studies found that the Young’s modulus of amorphous metal alloys can be predicted using only two effective macroscopic parameters. Although compositional descriptors were included, they proved ineffective—rendering the relationship essentially a macroscopic-to-macroscopic property correlation, which may be attributed to the limited microstructural variability typical of bulk metallic glasses compared to other alloy classes such as steels or superalloys [ 26 ]. ML-based methods that utilize neural networks (NNs) [ 27 ,  28 ], manifold learning and out-of-sample extension techniques such as diffusion maps (DM) and geometric harmonics (GH) [ 29 ,  30 – 31 ], and more recent frameworks such as double diffusion maps (DDM) [ 32 ] offer promising capabilities to extract latent correlations across diverse property spaces. However, the success of such models often hinges on the quality and completeness of input data, including factors like processing history that are known to significantly influence strength and durability [ 33 ,  34 ].

In this work, we address these challenges by analyzing a curated set of 1731 experimentally validated alloys from the ANSYS GRANTA database [ 35 ]. To the best of our knowledge, this dataset has not been previously used to train models for predicting and correlating material properties across such a diverse range of alloys. We categorize the dataset properties into thermal, mechanical, and strength-related groups, and systematically evaluate the ability of NN, GH, and DDM models to predict inter-property relationships. Our results reveal strong correlations between thermal and mechanical properties, but highlight the limitations of modeling strength behavior without incorporating post-processing treatments and their associated metadata. By integrating treatment data and metrics related to annealing, aging, and cooling for a subset of iron-based alloys, we demonstrate substantial gains in model performance in predicting material strength properties. These cross-property predictions are practically valuable for alloy systems that are data-scarce (limited measured properties), legacy (older or incomplete datasets), or proprietary (non-disclosed composition), where conventional modeling approaches relying on composition or microstructure are not applicable. By enabling reliable inference of unmeasured macroscopic properties from limited experimental inputs, this framework supports accelerated material evaluation and reduces the need for exhaustive property testing in partially characterized alloy systems.

The paper is outlined as follows: Sect. “ Dataset Description and Curation ” provides an overview of the dataset that was investigated in this study. Section “ Machine Learning Methods ” introduces the data-driven methods and frameworks that were utilized to predict alloy properties. Section “ Results and Discussion ” demonstrates and discusses the property prediction results achieved both with and without accounting for treatment and processing effects. Section “ Conclusion ” summarizes the findings of the work and discusses future opportunities with more robust datasets.

sections.heading: Dataset Description and Curation
paragraphs: The dataset utilized in this study is sourced from the ANSYS GRANTA Materials Universe database [ 35 ], comprising detailed experimental data for 1860 alloys. This dataset captures a wide range of metals and ductile alloys, covering lightweight high-strength aluminum alloys, superalloys, and refractory alloys. It provides a rich set of 26 + material properties that are essential for alloy characterization.

These properties include density  ρ , Young’s modulus  E , flexural modulus  E f , shear modulus  G , bulk modulus  K , Poisson’s ratio  ν , yield strength Ys, tensile strength Ts, compressive strength Cs, flexural strength Ms, Vickers hardness  H , fatigue strength Fs, thermal shock resistance  T sh , melting point Tm, thermal conductivity  k , specific heat capacity cp, thermal expansion coefficient  α , and latent heat of fusion  L f .

Each of these properties plays a significant role in understanding alloy performance. Density  ρ  represents the mass per unit volume, influencing weight-sensitive applications. Young’s modulus  E , flexural modulus  E f , and shear modulus  G  describe stiffness and resistance to deformation under different loading conditions, while the bulk modulus  K  reflects compressibility under uniform pressure. Poisson’s ratio  ν  captures lateral strain relative to axial strain under uniaxial stress. Yield strength Ys, tensile strength Ts, compressive strength Cs, and flexural strength Ms determine the mechanical performance of an alloy under different loading conditions. Hardness  H  quantifies resistance to surface deformation, while fatigue strength Fs assesses durability under cyclic loading. Thermal shock resistance  T sh  measures the material’s ability to withstand rapid temperature changes, crucial for applications exposed to extreme thermal fluctuations. Thermal properties such as melting point Tm, thermal conductivity  k , and specific heat capacity cp are crucial for high-temperature applications and heat transfer efficiency. The thermal expansion coefficient  α  describes dimensional changes with temperature variation, while latent heat of fusion  L f  highlights the energy required for phase transitions. For further details on the mechanical and thermal properties of alloys, readers are encouraged to refer to the following references [ 36 ,  37 ]. The dataset also contains additional properties that are derived from properties that are under investigation in this study, such as acoustic velocity, specific strength, and specific stiffness. However, properties such as elongation, toughness, fracture toughness, electrical conductivity, and the ductility index were not included in the scope of this work. Although available, these properties were excluded because they are governed by different physical mechanisms and exhibit strong sensitivity to processing and testing conditions; without consistent treatment metadata, they did not show a stable correlation structure with the thermal–mechanical-strength groups considered in this study. These properties will be considered in future work as more complete processing and testing metadata become available.

The original dataset of 1860 alloys was refined by filtering out entries with incomplete property data, resulting in a final dataset of 1731 alloys. Figure  1  illustrates the distribution of alloys categorized by their primary compositions. The dataset is dominated by iron-based alloys (669 entries), followed by aluminum alloys (310) and copper alloys (186). Other compositions, including nickel, titanium, and magnesium, contribute to the diversity, making this dataset highly representative of widely used engineering alloys. Fig. 1 Distribution of alloys in the ANSYS GRANTA dataset [ 35 ] based on their primary element

The correlation heatmap in Fig.  2  reveals distinct linear relationships among various material properties. The modulus properties—Young’s modulus  E , flexural modulus  E f , shear modulus G, and bulk modulus  K —exhibit strong positive correlations, reflecting their shared role in describing an alloy’s stiffness and resistance to deformation. Conversely, Poisson’s ratio  ν  is negatively correlated with the modulus properties, indicating its contrasting role in defining material deformation characteristics. This is expected from the theory of elasticity, where these moduli are interrelated through material constants and governed by assumptions of linear, isotropic elastic behavior [ 23 ]. Additionally, density  ρ  shows moderate correlations with these modulus properties, emphasizing the influence of atomic packing and composition on elastic behavior. Strength-related properties, including yield strength (Ys), tensile strength Ts, compressive strength Cs, flexural strength Ms, fatigue strength Fs, thermal shock resistance  T sh , and hardness H, exhibit strong intercorrelations. This suggests that alloys designed for high strength in one loading condition tend to retain superior performance across multiple stress states. Notably, thermal shock resistance  T sh  shows a strong correlation with tensile strength Ts, yield strength Ys, and hardness  H , indicating that materials resistant to thermal stress often possess high mechanical strength. Among thermal properties, the melting point Tm is positively correlated with the modulus properties, reflecting the influence of an alloy’s resistance to deformation on its thermal stability. However, thermal conductivity  k  and specific heat capacity cp) exhibit weaker correlations with other properties, suggesting complex dependencies beyond simple compositional trends. The thermal expansion coefficient ( α ) is negatively correlated with the modulus properties and melting point, indicating that materials with high stiffness and high melting temperatures tend to expand less with temperature changes. Lastly, latent heat of fusion L f  exhibits a moderate correlation with specific heat capacity cp, reinforcing its role in governing thermal energy storage and phase transformation behavior. Fig. 2 Heatmap illustrating the correlation between different properties within the ANSYS GRANTA dataset [ 35 ], along with the categorization of properties into mechanical, thermal, and strength groups. The last row also presents the normalized distributions of properties within each set

Based on the observed correlations and the relationships among properties, we categorized them into three main groups: Mechanical properties  Density ( ρ ), Young’s modulus ( E ), flexural modulus ( E f ), shear modulus ( G ), bulk modulus ( K ), and Poisson’s ratio ( ν ). Thermal properties  Melting point (Tm), thermal conductivity ( k ), specific heat capacity (cp), thermal expansion coefficient ( α ), and latent heat of fusion ( L f  ). Strength properties  Yield strength (Ys), tensile strength (Ts), compressive strength (Cs), flexural strength (Ms), Vickers hardness ( H ), fatigue strength (Fs), and thermal shock resistance (T sh ).

To further validate this categorization, Fig.  2  illustrates the distribution of each property set, normalized between 0 and 1. The strength properties follow a left-skewed distribution, while both mechanical and thermal properties exhibit a bimodal distribution. These distributions confirm that grouping properties into their respective sets based on the heatmap was an appropriate approach. Based on the correlation heatmaps and the distributions of each property, each property within a set can be expressed as a linear combination of others, whereas such relationships do not extend across different scales for most properties. This emphasizes the need for nonlinear methods to correlate the uncorrelated properties between different sets.

Mechanical and thermal properties of alloys are largely governed by their chemical composition, which makes it possible—with a suitable nonlinear model—to correlate them. In contrast, strength properties are significantly influenced not only by composition but also by microstructural factors. Since the dataset targets an industrial setting, microstructural information is not provided. However, the differences in microstructure are primarily attributed to treatment and processing methods, which can be used as a practical alternative to distinguish strength properties. These parameters modify the alloy’s internal structure to achieve desired mechanical characteristics, enabling cross-property correlations without relying on explicit microstructural data. These processes can be broadly categorized into cold working techniques and heat treatment methods. Cold working processes, which involve plastic deformation at low temperatures, include methods such as cold rolling [ 38 ] and cold drawing [ 39 ], among others, whereas heat treatment methods, which involve heating under specific conditions, encompass various processes, including annealing [ 40 ], normalizing [ 41 ], tempering [ 42 ], and aging [ 43 ], among others.

Each of these processes plays a crucial role in tailoring the mechanical properties of alloys for specific applications. The effect of these processes is what has caused the distribution of strength properties to appear different from the thermal and mechanical properties in Fig.  2 . Figure  3  highlights this effect by comparing strength properties across different processing conditions for two alloy groups. In Fig.  3 a, six variations of low-alloy steel AISI 9255 exhibit identical mechanical and thermal properties but differ significantly in strength properties due to differences in annealing, normalizing, quenching, and tempering processes. Similarly, in Fig.  3 b, various tempers of aluminum 6061 (T42, T451, T651, etc.) illustrate the impact of heat treatment on strength characteristics, while mechanical and thermal properties remain unchanged. These results emphasize the critical role of processing techniques in determining an alloy’s structural performance and highlight the challenge in modeling strength properties purely from composition data. Fig. 3 a  Six different low-alloy steel AISI 9255 samples from the ANSYS GRANTA dataset [ 35 ] exhibit identical normalized mechanical and thermal properties but differ in normalized strength properties due to variations in heat treatment.  b  Six different aluminum 6061 samples from the ANSYS GRANTA dataset [ 35 ] share the same normalized mechanical and thermal properties but show differences in normalized strength properties due to variations in tempering conditions

The ANSYS GRANTA database, with its extensive collection of experimentally validated alloy properties, provides a robust foundation for machine learning-driven materials property prediction. Many of these properties exhibit nonlinear correlations, with strength properties displaying unique variability due to the influence of heat treatment and processing, making their prediction inherently more complex than that of mechanical and thermal properties. Addressing this challenge requires advanced modeling techniques capable of capturing nonlinearities, thereby offering pathways to correlate thermal, mechanical, and strength properties.

sections.heading: Machine Learning Methods
paragraphs: The relationships among mechanical, thermal, and strength-related properties in engineering alloys are inherently nonlinear, arising from complex dependencies on composition, microstructure, and processing history. As shown in Sect. “ Dataset Description and Curation ,” properties within each defined group (mechanical, thermal, and strength) exhibit strong linear correlation; however, correlations across different groups do not follow simple linear trends and display distinctly nonlinear structure. Traditional linear modeling approaches are therefore insufficient for capturing these cross-property dependencies. To accurately model and predict material behavior across multiple property domains, it is essential to employ nonlinear learning frameworks capable of representing such structure.

In this study, we leverage three complementary nonlinear approaches: a commonly used neural network (NN) architecture, along with two manifold-based state-of-the-art methods, geometric harmonics (GH) and double diffusion maps (DDM). These models were selected to balance predictive performance and geometric structure preservation in high-dimensional property space. Our primary objective is not to derive explicit closed-form physical equations, but to establish reliable cross-property mappings that enable accurate macroscopic inference across diverse alloys. This data-driven approach is particularly justified because different alloy families exhibit distinct cross-property trends, making single empirical correlations difficult to generalize across broad material classes.

sections.heading: Neural Networks (NNs)
paragraphs: As one of the most powerful and versatile families of algorithms in machine learning, NNs have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of applications [ 44 ,  45 ]. The basic structure of a NN is the single-layer perceptron, consisting of an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer, all fully interconnected. Within the hidden layer, each neuron aggregates the weighted inputs it receives from the preceding layer, adds a bias term, and passes the result through a nonlinear activation function [ 46 ]. This process enables the model to capture nonlinearity and complex feature interactions. Figure  4 -a provides schematic illustrations of both a single-layer perceptron and an individual neuron. Fig. 4 Schematic representation of  a  single neural network modeling, and  b  manifold-based spectral regression using geometric harmonics (top, orange) and double diffusion maps (bottom, teal). GH performs dimensionality expansion, while DDM performs dimensionality reduction followed by dimensionality expansion

In the initial configuration of artificial neural network (NN) models, all connection weights are randomly initialized. During training, these weights are iteratively updated to enhance the model’s predictive accuracy—a process referred to as learning. This optimization of weights is governed by a learning algorithm, with back-propagation being the most widely adopted approach [ 47 ]. Introduced and popularized by Rumelhart et al., the back-propagation algorithm forms the core of many modern neural network implementations.

As its name implies, a back-propagation neural network (BPNN) propagates the prediction error backward through the network. Each neuron in the hidden layers receives error feedback from subsequent layers, enabling local updates based on their contribution to the overall prediction error [ 48 ]. This mechanism allows the model to fine-tune its internal parameters using the gradient descent method, whereby the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight is computed and used to reduce the error iteratively. The degree to which each neuron influences the final output loss is quantified through this gradient-based feedback, allowing weights  w i  and bias terms  b  to be refined at each iteration. A detailed explanation of the back-propagation learning algorithm and its implementation can be found in [ 45 ].

Our implementation for the neural network (NN) was done using the TensorFlow library [ 49 ]. Its architecture consisted of an input layer whose dimensionality varied depending on the selected catalog of input properties, followed by two hidden layers with 16 neurons each, and a single-neuron output layer corresponding to the target property. To enhance generalization and mitigate overfitting, a dropout layer was integrated between the hidden layers. All hidden layers employed the rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function [ 50 ], and the model was trained using the Adam optimizer with the mean-squared error (MSE) as the loss function. Input and output features were standardized using StandardScaler from the scikit-learn (sklearn) library [ 51 ]. For each target property, the dataset was randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing, and a fivefold cross-validation strategy was used to ensure robust model evaluation. An early stopping criterion was applied to terminate training if the validation loss did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs, with training running up to a maximum of 500 epochs. The trained model is publicly available on the GitHub link 1

sections.heading: Geometric Harmonics (GH)
paragraphs: Our implementation of the geometric harmonics (GH) algorithm was carried out using the datafold Python library [ 52 ]. Prior to training, both input and output features were standardized using StandardScaler from the scikit-learn (sklearn) library [ 51 ]. For each target property, the dataset was randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing subsets using a fixed random seed to ensure reproducibility. The GH model was constructed using a Gaussian kernel with a bandwidth parameter  ε  = 5, and the number of eigenpairs retained for interpolation was set to  k  = 80. Additionally, the density normalization bias parameter was set to  α  = 1, which effectively factors out the influence of non-uniform sampling density. The trained model is accessible on the previous GitHub link.

sections.heading: Double Diffusion Maps (DDM)
paragraphs: Double diffusion maps (DDM) is a two-stage interpolation scheme that combines manifold-based dimensionality reduction with the construction of a spectral basis for function extension [ 29 ,  30 ,  32 ]. While geometric harmonics (GH) performs function interpolation directly in the input space using a full set of eigenvectors—including both harmonic and non-harmonic components—DDM restricts its operation to a com-pressed latent space. This is accomplished by first reducing the dimensionality of the data using diffusion maps [ 29 ], followed by the construction of a new spectral basis for interpolation, analogous to geometric harmonics[ 30 ], using the leading non-harmonic components—referred to as latent harmonics [ 32 ].

The diffusion maps component is similar in formulation to GH: A local similarity kernel is computed, a normalization step is performed to account for sampling density, and an eigen decomposition yields the eigenvectors of the transition matrix. However, unlike GH, which retains all eigenvectors for functional approximation, diffusion

This two-stage scheme thus retains the manifold geometry via dimensionality reduction while enabling interpolation through a learned spectral basis in the latent space. Compared to GH, which performs function approximation using all eigenvectors in the ambient space, DDM achieves a more compact and generalizable representation by reconstructing the functional extension from fewer coordinates. As illustrated in Fig.  4 -b (bottom path, teal), the DDM pipeline first compresses the data into a latent embedding, then applies regression using the latent harmonics basis. This separation of geometry encoding and function extension not only reduces redundancy but also allows interpolation to be performed robustly in the vicinity of the training manifold, even for previously unseen inputs. For more details on double diffusion maps, the reader is encouraged to consult the following resource [ 32 ].

The double diffusion maps (DDM) algorithm was implemented using the datafold library [ 52 ]. A Gaussian kernel with bandwidth  ε  = 5 was used for both stages. sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: To evaluate the ability of machine learning models to capture relationships among different property categories, each model was trained using one complete set of properties as input to predict individual properties from the remaining two sets. This process was repeated across all combinations of input–output pairs. For each prediction task, the dataset was randomly split into 80% for training and 20% for testing to avoid overfitting and ensure robustness of the results. The predictive performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) on the testing data. To establish a meaningful benchmark, we consider a prediction to be reliable when  R 2  > 0 . 8, indicating a strong correlation between predicted and actual values.

sections.heading: Prediction Without Treatment and Processing Effects
paragraphs: In this first part of the analysis, we assess model performance without explicitly incorporating alloy treatment and processing effects. The parity plots corresponding to these prediction tasks are provided in the online supplementary material. sections.heading: Mechanical Properties from Thermal Properties
paragraphs: DDM consistently outperforms NN and GH across nearly all mechanical property predictions, achieving  R 2  > 0 . 8 for all six mechanical properties. It yields the highest accuracy for Young’s modulus (0 . 9549), flexural modulus (0 . 9640), shear modulus (0 . 9696), and bulk modulus (0 . 8933). GH performs slightly better than NN for density (0 . 9382 vs. 0 . 9248) but generally underperforms compared to DDM. Poisson’s ratio, though less predictable overall, still reaches  R 2  = 0 . 8159 under DDM.

sections.heading: Thermal Properties from Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: DDM also demonstrates strong predictive capabilities in this direction, achieving  R 2  > 0 . 8 for all five thermal properties. It leads in predicting melting point (0 . 9398), specific heat capacity (0 . 9467), and latent heat of fusion (0 . 9378). Thermal expansion coefficient (0 . 8388) and thermal conductivity (0 . 7980) are also well modeled. GH shows variable performance, dropping below the reliability threshold for thermal conductivity (0 . 5072). NN performs well in predicting specific heat capacity (0 . 9616) but is outperformed by DDM in most other cases.

sections.heading: Strength Properties from Thermal Properties
paragraphs: Strength properties are more difficult to predict using only thermal inputs, as none of the models achieve reliable performance based on the  R 2  > 0 . 8 benchmark. This outcome reflects the absence of critical information related to alloy processing. Among the models, DDM generally performs better than NN and GH, while GH consistently yields the lowest accuracy across this task.

sections.heading: Strength Properties from Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: A similar pattern emerges when predicting strength properties from mechanical features. While DDM generally performs better than the other models, and NN shows competitive performance in some cases, none of the models achieve the  R 2  > 0 . 8 threshold. These results further underscore the importance of incorporating processing and treatment variables, which play a critical role in determining the strength behavior of alloys.

The results indicate that double diffusion maps (DDM) was the most effective model for predicting both mechanical and thermal properties. This is because, unlike geometric harmonics (GH) and neural networks (NN), which operate in the full input space and tend to retain redundant or noisy information, DDM separates geometry encoding from function extension. This two-stage architecture enables it to capture global trends and local variations more effectively.

In contrast, none of the models were able to reliably predict strength properties from either mechanical or thermal inputs. As discussed in Sect. “ Dataset Description and Curation ,” this limitation is attributed to the influence of treatment and processing methods—many alloys share similar thermal and mechanical characteristics but exhibit significant differences in strength due to variations in heat treatment and cold working. Moreover, none of the models were able to reliably predict strength properties from either mechanical or thermal inputs. As discussed in Sect. “ Dataset Description and Curation ,” this limitation arises because strength is influenced not only by composition but also by microstructure. As a result, alloys with similar mechanical and thermal properties can differ significantly in strength. Since the focus is not to include explicit compositional or microstructural information, treatment and processing methods serve as critical bridging parameters, distinguishing alloys with similar input properties but varying strength characteristics due to differences in heat treatment or cold working.

sections.heading: Prediction With Treatment and Processing Effects
paragraphs: Since complete treatment process data were not available for all alloys in the dataset, we focused on iron-based (Fe) alloys, for which information can be collected from publicly accessible industrial standards and practices found online. The objective was to demonstrate the conceptual impact of incorporating treatment-related features into property prediction. The treatment process was represented using the following parameters: annealed, normalized, tempered, aged, tempering temperature, aging temperature, cold work, and cooling type. Among these, annealed, normalized, tempered, aged, and cold work were encoded as binary variables (0 or 1), indicating the presence or absence of each process. Tempering and aging temperatures were treated as continuous variables. Cooling type was encoded as a categorical variable with four discrete classes: air cooled, furnace cooled, oil quenched, and water quenched. While the complete preparation of alloys often involves additional details, such as normalizing and tempering temperatures, heating time, cooling time, and other treatment steps, this study focused only on the early mentioned parameters due to data availability and consistency across sources.

To assess the effect of incorporating this additional processing information, we compared the predictive performance of the three models—neural networks (NNs), geometric harmonics (GH), and double diffusion maps (DDM)—for Fe alloys, with and without the inclusion of treatment parameters. Table  2  summarizes the  R 2  values for predicting strength properties from either mechanical or thermal properties. The parity plots corresponding to these predictions with the inclusion of treatment and processing effects, along with the reported  R 2  values, are provided in the online supplementary material. sections.heading: Strength Properties from Thermal Properties
paragraphs: As seen from Table  2 , the inclusion of treatment-related features led to a significant performance improvement across all three models. For instance, the NN model improved from an average  R 2  of 0.4663 (without treatment) to 0.8407 (with treatment), corresponding to an 80.3% increase. Similar gains were observed for GH and DDM: GH rose from 0.5106 to 0.8330 (a 63.1% increase), while DDM increased from 0.3419 to 0.7096 (a 107.5% increase). Although not all predictions surpassed the reliability threshold of  R 2  > 0.8, several exceeded this threshold, indicating that treatment information provides a critical missing link for capturing the nonlinear factors governing strength behavior.

sections.heading: Strength Properties from Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Similar trends were observed when strength properties were predicted from mechanical inputs. The NN model improved from an average  R 2  of 0.4719 to 0.7843 (a 66.2% increase), while GH rose from 0.5627 to 0.7948 (a 41.2% increase), and DDM from 0.4383 to 0.8008 (an 82.7% increase). These results further demonstrate that mechanical properties alone are not sufficient to capture the full variation in strength properties without incorporating treatment information. The gains are especially pronounced for yield strength, where the predictions moved substantially closer to the target  R 2  = 0.8.

Overall, the inclusion of treatment and processing effects markedly improves the predictability of strength-related properties. While it is well established in metallurgy that strength is governed by microstructure and therefore depends on processing history, our results quantitatively demonstrate that this dependence also fundamentally limits the prediction of strength when only composition-derived thermal and mechanical descriptors are available. In this sense, treatment parameters serve as practical surrogates for microstructural information, consistent with prior studies showing that heat treatment and processing history strongly influence the resulting microstructure and, consequently, the measured properties [ 54 ,  55 ]. Importantly, our findings extend this principle beyond conventional composition–property relationships by showing that reliable correlations between distinct macroscopic property groups likewise require processing-aware inputs. This highlights a key contribution of the present work: providing a data-driven framework that explicitly reveals where these predictive relationships break down and how incorporating treatment metadata restores predictive capability, even when compositional or microstructural details are inaccessible. Such treatment-aware modeling enables accelerated property completion and screening in data-scarce, legacy, or proprietary alloy systems, where full characterization is impractical. sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This work investigated whether macroscopic thermal, mechanical, and strength properties of engineering alloys can be directly related using only experimentally measured properties, without relying on compositional or microstructural descriptors. Rather than pursuing traditional composition-to-property modeling, we focused on identifying transferable property-to-property relationships that enable macroscopic inference in partially characterized materials.

A central outcome of this study is that thermal and mechanical properties exhibit robust nonlinear correlations across diverse alloy classes, allowing reliable mutual prediction using data-driven models. In contrast, strength properties cannot be inferred from thermal or mechanical descriptors alone, even when advanced nonlinear learning frameworks are employed. While it is well established in metallurgy that strength is governed by microstructure and processing history, our results quantitatively demonstrate how this dependence fundamentally limits property-based inference when composition and microstructure are unavailable. By incorporating treatment metadata for Fe alloys, we show that processing-aware inputs restore predictive capability, confirming that treatment parameters act as practical surrogates for microstructural information in industrial datasets and clarifying how established metallurgical principles manifest within data-driven property correlation frameworks.

The machine learning models employed—neural networks, geometric harmonics, and double diffusion maps—were selected to capture nonlinear relationships across heterogeneous property spaces, with an emphasis on predictive accuracy rather than closed-form interpretability. This choice reflects the primary objective of the study: enabling reliable macroscopic property inference across diverse alloy systems, where simple empirical equations fail to generalize and incomplete characterization is common. From a practical perspective, this framework supports property completion in data-scarce, legacy, or proprietary alloy systems, where chemistry and processing may be known but comprehensive mechanical testing is unavailable or impractical. By inferring unmeasured macroscopic properties from limited experimental inputs, the approach reduces dependence on exhaustive testing while remaining compatible with industrial data constraints.

Future work will benefit from broader datasets that systematically document processing histories across multiple alloy families, allowing treatment-aware macroscopic inference to be extended beyond Fe-based systems. Such datasets will further clarify the limits and opportunities of property-driven modeling in materials engineering and strengthen the integration of experimental data with predictive analytics.
